Beth-peor
beth-PEE-or
proper noun
From the Hebrew, meaning “house of Peor”, named for the heathen god Baal-peor worshipped there, from a root meaning to open wide.

📖 Biblical Definition

Beth-peor was a place in the land of Moab, east of the Jordan, in the valley over against which Israel encamped in the last days before they crossed into Canaan. It lay in the inheritance afterward given to the tribe of Reuben (Jos 13:20). Moses recalled that “we abode in the valley over against Bethpeor” (Deu 3:29), and it was there, in the plains of Moab, that he delivered the great expositions of the law that fill Deuteronomy. The most solemn association of Beth-peor is the burial of Moses himself: “he buried him in a valley in the land of Moab, over against Bethpeor: but no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day” (Deu 34:6). The LORD hid the grave of His servant, that Israel might not make an idol of the place. For Beth-peor was already shadowed by idolatry, taking its very name from Baal-peor, to whom Israel joined themselves in the sin of Peor, committing whoredom with the daughters of Moab and bowing to their gods, for which a plague slew twenty and four thousand (Num 25:1–9). Thus Beth-peor holds together the giving of the law, the death of the lawgiver, and the memory of a grievous apostasy — a place where God’s word, God’s servant, and man’s idolatry meet, and where the hidden grave warns against turning even holy memory into a snare.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A place in Moab opposite which Israel camped, near Moses’ unknown grave, named for the idol Baal-peor.

expand to see more

BETH-PEOR, a place in the land of Moab, east of Jordan, in Reuben’s allotment.

Israel abode in the valley over against it before crossing Jordan (Deu 3:29).

Moses was buried in a valley over against it, his grave unknown (Deu 34:6).

It took its name from Baal-peor, the idol of the sin of Peor (Num 25:3).

It fell within the inheritance of the tribe of Reuben (Jos 13:20).

📖 Key Scripture

Deu 3:29 — "So we abode in the valley over against Bethpeor."

Deu 34:6 — "And he buried him in a valley in the land of Moab, over against Bethpeor: but no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day."

Jos 13:20 — "And Bethpeor, and Ashdothpisgah, and Bethjeshimoth,"

Num 25:3 — "And Israel joined himself unto Baalpeor: and the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The lesson to recover is that idolatry brings plague and death, and that God hides even holy memorials lest they become idols.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The lesson to recover from Beth-peor is the deadliness of idolatry. There Israel joined itself to Baal-peor, and the anger of the LORD burned, and a plague slew thousands. The sin of Peor became a standing warning against the lust and false worship that seduce the covenant people at the very threshold of blessing.

There is a second mercy at Beth-peor. The LORD buried His servant Moses and hid the grave, that Israel might not make a shrine of it. So jealous is God for true worship that He will conceal even the resting place of His greatest prophet rather than let it become a snare. The believer learns to cling to the living God Himself, not to relics, places, or sacred memories.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The name means “house of Peor,” binding the place to the idol Baal-peor worshipped in that valley.

expand to see more

Beth-peor — “house of Peor,” from the idol of that name.

Beth means “house” and Peor names the Moabite god.

The god’s name may derive from a root meaning to open or gape.

It is bound to Mount Peor, where Balaam looked upon Israel (Num 23:28).

The name itself preaches the idolatry the place is remembered for.

Usage

"Israel encamped in the valley over against Beth-peor."

"Moses was buried near Beth-peor, and no man knows the place."

"The sin of Beth-peor brought a plague upon the camp of Israel."
